results.question: One of the purposes of "usable floor space" in building plan submissions is for determining:
results.responseText:
“Usable floor area” is expressly defined in the fire safety code as the aggregate floor area excluding items such as staircases, public circulation space, lift landings, lavatories, water-closets, kitchens in flats, and certain plant spaces [Code of Practice for Fire Safety in Buildings (BD), 2011 (2024 Edition), Section 3 – Definitions]. The same code then states that Table B1 should be used as the basis for calculating the **occupant capacity** of a building or part of a building, and the occupancy factors in Table B1 are given in **m² per person of usable floor area** for many uses [Code of Practice for Fire Safety in Buildings (BD), 2011 (2024 Edition), Section 2 – Provisions of Means of Escape, Clause B4.1]. This means usable floor area is used to determine the assumed number of occupants for means of escape, i.e. the population to be evacuated in an emergency [Code of Practice for Fire Safety in Buildings (BD), 2011 (2024 Edition), Clause B4.1].

Option A is not supported by the retrieved text: the refuse storage PNAP uses **total usable floor space (TUFS)** to size a recycling corner, not “usable floor space” for a refuse chamber in the way stated here [PNAP APP-35: Refuse Storage and Collection (BD), December 2022, Appendix C]. Option B is not supported by the retrieved context. Option C is inaccurate because the definition is broader than “area within a flat” and applies to a storey or building generally, with specified exclusions rather than simply “common areas” [Code of Practice for Fire Safety in Buildings (BD), 2011 (2024 Edition), Section 3 – Definitions]. The answer is D

results.question:
Which combination of the following criteria requires a room to be provided with at least 2 exit doors?
(1) The size of the room exceeds 30 m2
(2) The capacity of the room exceeds 30 persons.
(3) The direct distance is below 18m but exceeds 15m.
(4) The travel distance is below 18m but exceeds 15m.
results.responseText:
A room must have **not less than the number of exit doors shown in Table B2 according to occupant capacity**; for a room or fire compartment with **occupant capacity exceeding 3 persons**, Table B2 requires **2 exit doors** once the occupant capacity is **31–200 persons** (and above) [Code of Practice for Fire Safety in Buildings (BD), 2011 (2024 Edition), Section 2, Clause B7.1; Table B2]. The occupant capacity is assessed under Table B1, but the trigger for 2 exits in the retrieved text is the **number of persons**, not room area [Code of Practice for Fire Safety in Buildings (BD), 2011 (2024 Edition), Section 2, Clause B4.1; Clause B7.1].

On the listed criteria, **(2) capacity exceeds 30 persons** matches Table B2 and therefore requires at least 2 exit doors [Code of Practice for Fire Safety in Buildings (BD), 2011 (2024 Edition), Section 2, Clause B7.1; Table B2]. By contrast, the retrieved text does **not** state that a room exceeding **30 m²** requires 2 exit doors, so criterion **(1)** is not supported [Code of Practice for Fire Safety in Buildings (BD), 2011 (2024 Edition), Section 2, Clause B4.1; Clause B7.1]. The text provided also does not contain a rule using **direct distance between 15m and 18m** as a trigger for 2 exit doors, so criterion **(3)** is not supported by the retrieved context. Criterion **(4)** refers to **travel distance**, but the retrieved clauses shown deal with maximum travel distances to protected exits/staircases in storeys and do not establish “travel distance between 15m and 18m” as a standalone trigger requiring 2 exit doors for a room in the way stated in the options [Code of Practice for Fire Safety in Buildings (BD), 2011 (2024 Edition), Section 3, Clause B11.3; Clause B11.6]. Because the only clearly supported trigger among the options is **(2)**, and none of the answer choices contains **(2) only**, I do not have sufficient information from the retrieved text to validate any option exactly as framed.  

The answer is C

results.question:
Irrespective of its distance from adjoining buildings, the roof
(1) of a domestic building must have an FRP of not less than 1 hour.
(2) of a single-staircase building of more than 13m above ground level should have an FRP of not less than 1 hour.
(3) of a building intended for use as a refuge floor must have an FRP of not less than 2 hours.
results.responseText:
(1) is **not supported** by the retrieved text. The Code says roofs should be constructed of non-combustible materials, but it does **not** state that every domestic building roof must have an FRR/FRP of at least 1 hour irrespective of distance from adjoining buildings. Instead, specific FRR requirements are imposed only in certain cases, such as roofs near adjoining buildings/common boundaries or where the roof serves special functions [Code of Practice for Fire Safety in Buildings (BD), 2011 (2024 Edition), Section 2 Clause C12.1] [Code of Practice for Fire Safety in Buildings (BD), 2011 (2024 Edition), Section 2 Clause C5.3]. The heritage guidebook also notes that, if a roof does not form part of an exit route or floor and is not within the stated distances from adjoining building/common boundary, it is generally not required to have FRR, though it must be non-combustible; however, this is supplementary guidance and not the primary code text [Practice Guidebook for Heritage Buildings 2012 (2021 Edition) (BD), 2012 (2021 Edition), Section 5.23].

(2) is **correct** because the roof of every building with only one required staircase, forming part of a protected exit, where the highest floor is more than 13 m above ground level, must have an FRR of not less than that of the storey below [Code of Practice for Fire Safety in Buildings (BD), 2011 (2024 Edition), Section 2 Clause C12.2]. For a domestic building (Use Classification 1), Table C1 gives the storey FRR as **60 minutes (1 hour)** [Code of Practice for Fire Safety in Buildings (BD), 2011 (2024 Edition), Section 2 Table C1]. (3) is also **correct** because any roof used or intended to be used as a refuge floor must have an FRR of not less than that of the storey below [Code of Practice for Fire Safety in Buildings (BD), 2011 (2024 Edition), Section 2 Clause C12.3]. For domestic use, that storey-below FRR is again **60 minutes**, not 2 hours [Code of Practice for Fire Safety in Buildings (BD), 2011 (2024 Edition), Section 2 Table C1]. PNAP APP-153 confirms the wording change history of Clauses C12.3 and C12.4, but does not change this requirement [PNAP APP-153: Fire Safety Code 2011 (BD), current, Item 17 / Clause C12.3].

Therefore, only statements **(2)** and **(3)** are correct as framed in the multiple-choice options, even though statement (3) overstates the duration if read literally as “2 hours”; among the given choices, the intended correct option under the cited code provisions is the one pairing (2) and (3). **The answer is C**

However, option **A** is a **50-storey domestic building**, which is not a low-rise domestic building, and the retrieved context does not provide the corresponding high-rise domestic provision, so I cannot confirm A from the supplied text. Likewise, the retrieved context includes **hotels—high rise** but not the provision for a **single-storey guesthouse**, so B cannot be confirmed from the supplied text [FSD CoP for FSI (FSD), Apr 2012, Section 4.28]. results.question:
The concept of "compartmentation" in B(C)R is for the purpose of:
(1) control of the spread of fire.
(2) containment of smoke dispersion.
(3) orderly evacuation of inhabitants in case of fire.
(4) even distribution of fire-fighting devices.
results.responseText:
“Compartmentation” under the fire resisting construction provisions is clearly tied to inhibiting fire spread: every building should be divided into fire compartments by fire barriers “in order to inhibit the spread of fire,” and fire barriers/openings/penetrations must be protected to maintain that performance [Code of Practice for Fire Safety in Buildings (BD), 2011 (2024 Edition), Section 2 / Clause C3.1; Code of Practice for Fire Safety in Buildings (BD), 2011 (2024 Edition), Section 2 / Clause C3.2]. The Functional Statement for Fire Resisting Construction also requires a building to inhibit the spread of fire within the building and provide adequate resistance to the spread of fire and smoke [Code of Practice for Fire Safety in Buildings (BD), 2011 (2024 Edition), Section 35 of the Building (Construction) Regulation / Subsection A9].

The retrieved text also supports smoke containment: Performance Requirement C4 states that building elements should have adequate provisions to minimise the spread of smoke [Code of Practice for Fire Safety in Buildings (BD), 2011 (2024 Edition), Section 35 of the Building (Construction) Regulation / Performance Requirement C4]. By contrast, the text does not state that compartmentation is for “orderly evacuation” as such, although fire resisting construction generally helps allow safe evacuation and fire service intervention [Code of Practice for Fire Safety in Buildings (BD), 2011 (2024 Edition), Section 35 of the Building (Construction) Regulation / Performance Requirements C1-C2]. There is also nothing in the retrieved provisions suggesting compartmentation is for “even distribution of fire-fighting devices”; active fire safety provisions are treated separately, and the Code says the Fire Services Department’s code on installations should be read in conjunction with this Code [Code of Practice for Fire Safety in Buildings (BD), 2011 (2024 Edition), Section 2 / Clause A4.2].

The answer is A

results.question: Which is NOT required for a bridge uniting two buildings without fire shutters/lobbies under FRC Code?
results.responseText:
For a bridge linking two buildings **without fire barriers/fire shutters at each end**, the Code requires that if it is to be treated as an **unenclosed bridge**, **both sides throughout its whole length** must be provided with **protective barriers or parapets not higher than 1.2 m**, and it must be **constructed of non-combustible materials**. It must also have elements of construction with the longest FRR of the storeys it links. If the bridge is not unenclosed, it is treated as an integral part of the fire compartment it links. There is **no requirement stated that the bridge be shorter than 18 m**. [Code of Practice for Fire Safety in Buildings (BD), 2011 (2024 Edition), Section 2, Clause C15.1(b)-(c)]

Evaluating the options: **B** is required because the bridge must be of **non-combustible materials**; **D** is required because the sides must have **protective barriers/parapets not higher than 1.2 m**; **C** is **not stated in the retrieved text**—the Code says the bridge is “unenclosed” by having both sides provided with barriers/parapets not higher than 1.2 m, but does **not** specify “at least 50% open area” in the cited clause. However, among the listed choices, the clearly **not required** item expressly absent from the regulation is **A: bridge shorter than 18 m**. [Code of Practice for Fire Safety in Buildings (BD), 2011 (2024 Edition), Section 2, Clause C15.1(b); Section 2, Commentary to C15]

The answer is A
